sections.h2: What heirs can owe on an inherited house
sections.html: Arizona doesn't levy an estate, inheritance or gift tax. Two things can still touch an heir: federal estate tax, which only hits very large estates, and income tax on any gain after a sale. Most families spend more energy on paperwork than on tax. You'll need to know who is allowed to sign, whether a court has to be involved, and how creditors get handled. A statute governs each, and skipping a step can stall a closing.

The IRS wants an estate tax return only when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, is larger than the cutoff for the year the person died. Simple estates rarely come close. The cutoffs, year by year:

Died inReturn required above
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

A surviving spouse can inherit the leftover exemption if the estate files a timely return and makes that choice. For the house, the number that matters is fair market value on the date of death. Whatever the owner originally paid is irrelevant. Even without a return, get a written appraisal or similar proof of that value.

sections.h2: Who can sell an inherited house
sections.html:
A deed is only good if signed by someone with legal authority, and right after a death that is rarely the relative who lives closest. Arizona usually points to one of three people: a court-appointed personal representative, a successor holding a recorded affidavit, or a beneficiary named in a recorded beneficiary deed. The way the owner held title tells you which.

Under A.R.S. 14-3715 a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease the estate's real property, for cash or on credit. They must act reasonably for the people with an interest, and a will or court order can cut the power back. Repairs, insurance, and payment of taxes and administration costs fall under the same grant.

Without an appointment there's no closing. Buyers and escrow officers will hold off, since no one can yet deliver good title.

sections.h2: Can heirs skip probate with an affidavit?
sections.html:
Some estates can. The route is an affidavit of succession for real property under A.R.S. 14-3971, and each of these requirements must be met:

  • At least six months have run since the death. A certified death certificate goes with the affidavit.
  • No one has applied for or received appointment as personal representative.
  • The real property is valued at $300,000 or less once liens and encumbrances are subtracted. The county assessment rolls for the year of death supply the full cash value used.
  • Funeral bills, last illness bills and every unsecured debt are paid off.
  • The signers are the heirs or devisees entitled to the property, and nobody else has a claim to it.
  • Federal estate tax doesn't apply.

The paperwork travels in two steps. The court in the county where the person lived receives the affidavit and issues a certified copy. You then take that copy to the recorder serving the house. Standard filing fees apply unless waived.

The statute also offers a second affidavit for personal property up to $200,000, usable after 30 days. That one suits a vehicle or bank accounts, and it can't move the house.

If the owner recorded a beneficiary deed, the person named in it receives the house when the owner dies and probate is avoided. A.R.S. 33-405 sets two conditions: the document says it takes effect at the owner's death, and it is signed and filed with the recorder of the county that holds the land, all before the owner passes away.

Heirs should know the following:

  • Whatever mortgages, liens and encumbrances were on the house at death remain on it.
  • Until death, the owner is free to cancel by recording a revocation.
  • Where several beneficiary deeds were recorded, the final one before death wins.
  • A will written afterward doesn't cancel it.
  • With no surviving grantee and no named successor beneficiary, the deed is void.

The beneficiary never had to sign or be informed while the owner lived, so a deed can come as a surprise. Look through the recorder's index early.

sections.h2: How long heirs can wait to open an estate
sections.html:
There's a two-year outer limit after death for starting most Arizona probate cases. A.R.S. 14-3108 bars informal probate or appointment, and formal testacy or appointment proceedings, once more than two years have gone by, subject to listed exceptions.

One exception opens the door to a late case if nothing was filed in court about succession or administration during those two years. In that situation the personal representative may keep estate assets only to the extent needed to confirm title with the rightful successors, and no claims can be presented except administration expenses.

When nobody administers the estate, A.R.S. 14-3901 has heirs and devisees take under the probated will or by intestacy. Administration charges, creditor claims, and allowances for a surviving spouse and dependent children still come first.

Debts of the person who died can follow the house to the heirs, so clear them before closing or at it. A.R.S. 14-3803 cuts off claims that existed before death if they aren't presented within two years of death plus any notice period, or sooner for creditors who got actual notice or publication.

Claims that come up at or after death, such as contract claims against the personal representative, must be presented within four months of the date performance is due or the claim arises. For other claims the two-year rule governs the later date. None of this limits enforcement of a mortgage or other lien on estate property, so a lender can still pursue the house.

sections.h2: What the recorder needs at closing
sections.html:
Recording a deed takes a completed affidavit of legal value. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, both sides, or their agents, certify the names and addresses, legal description, sale date, total consideration, financing type and the assessor's parcel number.

The form also asks if the buyer will live in the house or rent it out, and whether buyer and seller are related. A deed without a complete affidavit is refused unless it carries a listed exemption.

When the seller is an estate, bring proof of authority too, such as court letters or the recorded affidavit of succession. Your title company can give you its checklist at the start, which saves a second trip to the recorder.

Delays usually trace back to three things: nobody with signing authority, debts left unpaid, and a house left vacant. None of them are tax rules, yet each can hold up a closing.

  • No personal representative has been named, so no one can sign.
  • Heirs in different states must all agree.
  • A mortgage or lien outlives the owner and has to come out of the sale proceeds.
  • Back taxes or repairs built up while the house sat empty.
  • Nobody is sure of the date-of-death value.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it is, so you skip repairs. The title steps above still have to be completed.

A practical order of work helps. First find out how title was held and whether a beneficiary deed is on record. Next decide whether the estate fits the affidavit route or needs a personal representative. Then collect the death certificate, the date-of-death value and a list of debts, and finally call a title company to confirm what it needs. Doing these in sequence keeps a buyer from walking away over a missing signature.

faqs.q: Does Arizona charge an estate tax or inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. Arizona repealed its estate tax and has no inheritance or gift tax. Federal estate tax applies only above the filing threshold, which is $15,000,000 for a death in 2026.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited Arizona house without probate?
faqs.a: Yes, when title comes through a recorded beneficiary deed, or when the estate qualifies for an affidavit of succession (real property worth $300,000 or less after liens, and six months since the death). In other cases a court-appointed personal representative has to sign.

faqs.q: How long do I have to open probate in Arizona?
faqs.a: The general outer limit is two years from the date of death for most informal and formal proceedings. A.R.S. 14-3108 lists the exceptions.

faqs.q: Can a personal representative sell the house?
faqs.a: Yes, unless the will or a court order says otherwise. A.R.S. 14-3715 covers sale, mortgage or lease of estate real property for cash or credit.

faqs.q: What does the county recorder require for the sale?
faqs.a: An affidavit of legal value attached to the deed. It states the parties, legal description, date of sale, total consideration and type of financing.
